lessons.title: The Common Threads Behind Every Crash

body.text: Every crash has a different trigger but a familiar skeleton: a true story, easy money, leverage, a belief that this time is different, and a moment when forced sellers meet a market with no buyers.

children.text: Over the last four chapters you have lived through the Great Crash, Black Monday, the dot-com bust, the Global Financial Crisis, India's two great scams and the COVID crash. On the surface they look completely different: margin loans and ticker tape in 1929, computer models in 1987, fake bank receipts in 1992, subprime mortgages in 2008, a virus in 2020. This lesson strips away the details and lays the crashes side by side, so you can see the threads that run through almost all of them, and use those threads to judge the market you invest in today.
Six Crashes, Side by Side

body.text: Read down the columns rather than across the rows. The stories change completely. The fuel is almost always some form of borrowed or diverted money. The belief is almost always a version of "this time is different". And the amplifier is almost always selling that is forced, automatic or both.

children.text: Thread 1: It Starts With a True Story

No major crash in this course began with a lie that everyone could see through. The 1920s really did transform daily life. India's 1991 reforms really did unleash growth. The internet really did change the world. That is what makes bubbles so convincing: in the displacement stage from Lesson 1.2, the early believers are right, and they get rich. The danger arrives later, when the price paid for the story runs far ahead of what the story can deliver.
Thread 2: Easy Money Feeds the Fire

Almost every bubble in this course was financed by money that was cheap, borrowed or not really the investor's own. In 1929 it was brokers' loans. In 1992 it was bank funds routed through a broker's account. In 2000 and 2001 it was a flood of IPO capital and, in India, co-operative bank loans against inflated shares. In 2008 it was a 1% Fed rate and mortgages granted without income checks. Easy money does not cause a bubble on its own, but it lets prices rise far further, far faster, than savings alone ever could.
Thread 3: Leverage Turns Falls Into Wipeouts

Leverage appears in nearly every crash, wearing a different costume each time: margin accounts, pledged promoter shares, investment bank balance sheets, MTF positions and F&O contracts. The maths from Lesson 1.3 never changes.

body.caption: Ignoring interest and costs. The more leverage, the smaller the fall needed to lose everything.
How Small a Fall Is Fatal?

cells: An investor with no borrowing
1x
A trader using 5x MTF or intraday leverage
5x
A 1929 margin buyer with 10% down
Lehman Brothers in 2007, about 31 to 1
About 3.2%

body.title: Your Turn: Find the Breaking Point
body.prompt: A trader controls a ₹16 lakh position with ₹2 lakh of their own money, funded by borrowing and derivatives. Ignoring interest and costs, what percentage fall in the position wipes out their entire ₹2 lakh? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Leverage = ₹16 lakh ÷ ₹2 lakh = 8x. The wipeout fall is 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5%. A 12.5% fall on ₹16 lakh is ₹2 lakh, exactly the trader's capital. On 23 March 2020 alone, the Sensex fell 13.15%, so a position like this tracking the market would have been wiped out in a single day, long before the recovery began.

children.text: Thread 4: "This Time Is Different"

In their 2009 study of eight centuries of financial crises, economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff chose a title that captures the most dangerous belief in finance: This Time Is Different. Each bubble in this course had its own version of that belief, and each sounded reasonable at the time.
stock prices had reached a permanently high plateau, according to one of America's most respected economists.
one brilliant operator had cracked the market, so following the Big Bull was a safe bet.
in the new economy, profits no longer mattered, and users and eyeballs were what counted.
national house prices never fall, and India's economy had decoupled from the West.

body.title: Match the Belief
body.question: An analyst argues that traditional valuation measures are obsolete because a new technology has changed how companies make money, so revenue and user growth matter more than profits. Which crash does this reasoning most closely echo?
body.explanation: Dismissing profits in favour of revenue, users or "eyeballs" because of a new technology is the signature belief of the dot-com bubble, covered in Lesson 2.3. The technology can be real and the belief can still be dangerous, because it removes the anchor that tells you whether a price is too high.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff titled their study of eight centuries of financial crises This Time Is ___.
body.explanation: The title is ironic. In almost every era, investors convinced themselves that the old rules no longer applied, and in almost every era they were wrong. When you hear that phrase, or any version of it, treat it as a warning.

children.text: Thread 5: Hidden Links and Forced Sellers

markDefs.definition: Investors who must sell regardless of price, because of margin calls, loan terms, redemption requests or automatic risk rules.

children.text: Crashes become catastrophes when losses travel through connections nobody was watching. In 1929, margin calls hit banks. In 1992, a broker's account linked State Bank of India to share prices. In 2001, Ketan Parekh's losses reached co-operative bank depositors and UTI unitholders. In 2008, Lehman's failure reached a money market fund within a day and ICICI Bank's depositors within two weeks. At the bottom of every one of these crashes, prices were set not by investors calmly weighing value, but by
forced sellers
who had no choice, meeting buyers who had no confidence.
Thread 6: Trust Breaks, Then the Rules Change

Every crash in this course ended with new rules, because every crash exposed a gap that someone had exploited. The Securities and Exchange Commission came out of 1929. Circuit breakers came out of 1987. SEBI's powers, NSE and the demat system were built after 1992. Rolling settlement and the ban on badla came after 2001. Tougher bank regulation came after 2008. These reforms genuinely make markets safer. But notice the pattern: regulation almost always fixes the last crisis, while the next one tends to find a new gap.
The Exception: Crashes Without a Bubble

Not every crash follows the full pattern. The 2020 crash was mainly an external shock that hit a market without a single dominant bubble or a banking system stuffed with bad loans. That difference shows up clearly in how quickly markets recovered.

columns.label: Bubble Crash
points: Builds over years, as a story, easy money and leverage push prices far above value
Losses reach banks and the wider financial system
Prices must fall back to value, and often below it
Recovery can take many years, or even decades

columns.label: Shock Crash
points: Arrives suddenly from outside the market, such as a pandemic or a war
The financial system enters the crisis in reasonable health
Prices fall on fear and uncertainty, not because they were wildly overvalued
With strong policy support, recovery can be fast

body.title: Years to Regain the Pre-Crash Peak

body.label: The Recovery Rule of Thumb
body.value: The bigger the bubble, the longer the wait
body.context: The two biggest bubbles in this course, 1929 and 2000, took about 25 and 15 years to regain their peaks. The 2020 shock crash took under a year. How much a market was overvalued going in matters as much as how far it falls.

children.text: A Warning Sign Scorecard for Indian Markets

You cannot predict when the next crash will come. But you can check how many of the common threads are present in the market today. The more threads you see at once, the more fragile the market is likely to be.

body.caption: Crash Thread Scorecard: What to Check in India

cells: Stretched valuations
Nifty PE far above its own long-term history, using the same calculation method
Nifty Indices historical PE data
Leverage
Rapid growth in MTF borrowing, F&O trading volumes and promoter pledging
NSE and SEBI data, Screener.in shareholding pages
IPO and SME frenzy
Record oversubscription, loss-making issuers and big listing day pops
NSE and BSE IPO pages, subscription data
First-time investor rush and tips
Surging new demat accounts, stock tips in social media and messaging groups
Depository data, news reports
"This time is different"
Arguments that valuations, profits or cycles no longer matter
Financial media, broker reports, social media
Hidden links
Stress in non-bank lenders, debt funds or other interconnected institutions
RBI Financial Stability Report

body.title: Score Today's Market
steps: Look up the current Nifty 50 PE and compare it with its own long-term average under the same method
Check recent news or data on MTF borrowing and F&O trading volumes
Review the last three months of IPOs and SME IPOs: subscription levels and how many issuers were loss-making
Note whether friends, family or social media are sharing stock tips more than usual
Look for any widely repeated argument that "this time is different"
Skim the latest RBI Financial Stability Report summary for risks it highlights
Count how many of the six threads you see clearly today, and write down the date and your score to revisit in six months

body.title: Why the Scorecard Cannot Time a Crash

children.text: Spotting warning signs is not the same as predicting a crash. Markets can stay expensive, leveraged and euphoric for much longer than seems reasonable.
The famous early warning:

in December 1996, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan publicly questioned whether "irrational exuberance" had pushed up asset prices. The Nasdaq kept rising for more than three years before its March 2000 peak.
The cost of selling too early:
an investor who sold everything on that warning would have been right about the bubble and still missed years of gains, possibly ending up buying back higher.
What the scorecard is for:
not deciding when to sell everything, but deciding how much risk to take, how much leverage to avoid, and how prepared to be.
Lesson 5.3 turns this idea into a practical portfolio framework.

body.title: Record Highs and Rising Nerves
body.scenario: The Nifty has just hit a record high. Your cousin, who has taken this course, messages you: "I can see at least four of the six crash threads right now. Valuations look stretched, SME IPOs are getting hundreds of times oversubscribed, everyone in my office is trading options, and people keep saying India is different this time. Should I sell all my mutual funds and wait for the crash?"
body.prompt: How would you respond, using the ideas from this lesson?
body.modelAnswer: Your cousin is doing exactly the right thing by noticing the threads, but drawing the wrong conclusion from them. The scorecard measures fragility, not timing. As the Greenspan example shows, markets can stay stretched for years, and selling everything now could mean missing substantial gains and then buying back at higher prices, which is the same outcome as panic selling at the bottom. A better response is to use the warning signs to prepare rather than predict. First, avoid adding leverage: no MTF, no F&O positions they cannot afford to lose. Second, check that their asset allocation matches their goals and time horizon, and rebalance if equities have grown well beyond their target share because of the rally. Third, stay away from the most frothy parts of the market, such as SME IPOs and hyped themes, where the threads are strongest. Fourth, make sure their emergency fund is separate and adequate, so they will never be a forced seller. Finally, write down now what they will do if the market falls 30% or 40%, so a future crash triggers a plan rather than panic. Being cautious in a frothy market is sensible. Betting everything on a crash arriving soon is just another form of prediction.

body.title: Which Thread Was Missing?
body.question: Which common thread was largely missing from the COVID crash of March 2020, helping explain its fast recovery?
options: A long, leverage-fuelled bubble with a banking system full of bad loans
A sharp rise in fear, as measured by India VIX
A strong policy response from RBI and the government
body.explanation: March 2020 had plenty of forced selling, record fear and a strong policy response. What it lacked was the slow build-up of a huge, leveraged bubble that left banks holding bad loans, as in 1929 or 2008. Without that damage to fix, markets could recover once the immediate panic eased and policy support arrived.

body.label: Reserve Bank of India: Financial Stability Report
body.description: RBI publishes a Financial Stability Report twice a year, assessing risks to India's banks, non-bank lenders and markets. Search for the latest edition on RBI's website and read the overview chapter.

cards.definition: Bubbles begin with a real change, such as the internet or economic reform, which makes early optimism look justified.
Cheap or borrowed money, from margin loans to low interest rates, lets prices rise far beyond what savings alone could support.
Borrowing multiplies losses. The fall that wipes out equity is 100 divided by the leverage.
A belief that old valuation rules no longer apply, from the "permanent plateau" of 1929 to the "new economy" of 2000.

cards.term: Thread 5: Hidden Links and Forced Sellers
cards.definition: Losses spread through unseen connections, and forced sellers push prices below value at the bottom.
Each crash exposes a gap and brings reforms, but new crises tend to find new gaps.
Bubble crashes, such as 1929 and 2000, recover slowly. Shock crashes into a healthy system, such as 2020, can recover fast.

points: Crashes differ in their triggers but share a common skeleton: a true story, easy money, leverage, "this time is different" thinking, hidden links and forced sellers
Leverage turns falls into wipeouts: the fall that destroys equity is 100 divided by the leverage, just 10% at 10x and about 3.2% at 31x
Every major crash produced reforms, from the SEC to SEBI's powers and India's demat system, but regulation tends to fix the last crisis rather than the next
Bubble crashes recover slowly, taking about 25 years after 1929 and 15 after 2000, while the 2020 shock crash recovered in under a year
A warning sign scorecard helps you judge how fragile a market is, but it cannot tell you when a crash will come
Use warning signs to prepare, by limiting leverage, keeping an emergency fund and planning ahead, not to predict and bet everything on timing

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The scorecard is a learning framework, not a trading signal or a prediction tool. Historical recovery periods are approximate and depend on the index and dates used.
